name: Jacob
desc: Son of Isaac; renamed Israel; father of the twelve tribes
christ_connection: Jacob, the son of Isaac and father of the twelve tribes, is typified in the New Testament as the precursor to Christ, whose journey and faith mirror Jacob's covenantal faith and perseverance. His wrestling with God in Gilead (Genesis 32:22-32) is a profound typology of Christ's struggle with God in the Garden of Gethsemane, where He bears the weight of sin and is ultimately reconciled through His sacrifice. Jacob's renaming of himself to Israel (Genesis 35:10) prefigures the New Covenant name of Christ, which signifies the new people of God. As the patriarch who entered into a covenant with God, Jacob's life exemplifies the covenantal faith essential for the salvation of the elect, and his story is a foundational narrative in the arc of sacred history leading to the fulfillment in Christ.

name: David
desc: Shepherd-king of Israel; ancestor of Jesus Christ
christ_connection: David, as the shepherd-king of Israel, typifies the role of a righteous leader who seeks to preserve the covenant of God with His people. His lineage, traced through Jesse and ultimately through Jesus Christ, underscores the fulfillment of the covenantal promise made to Abraham. The psalms attributed to David, such as Psalm 2 and Psalm 110, prophesy of the coming of a Messiah who would reign over Israel and fulfill the divine purpose of salvation. The covenantal relationship established through David's reign is a foundational element in the narrative of salvation history, illustrating how the typological structure of the Old Testament points toward the eternal covenant with Jesus Christ.

name: Moses
desc: Deliverer of Israel; received the law on Sinai
christ_connection: Moses, as the deliverer of Israel and the recipient of the law on Sinai, typifies the role of a prophet-king who mediates between God and His people. His commissioning by God in Exodus 4:10-13 parallels Jesus' anointing by the Father in John 13:16, both of which signify the inauguration of a new covenant. The covenantal relationship established through Moses' mediation, as seen in Deuteronomy 7:1-15, anticipates the fulfillment of Jesus as the ultimate mediator of the new covenant, where the law is no longer given but the Spirit is imparted (Hebrews 8:6-7). The sacrificial death of Moses, as recounted in Numbers 20:22-23, prefigures the sacrificial death of Jesus, who is the Lamb of God (Hebrews 10:12). Thus, Moses serves as a type of Christ, through whom the law is made obsolete and the new covenant is inaugurated.

name: Jacob
desc: Son of Lehi; taught pure doctrine of Christ; author of the book of Jacob
christ_connection: Jacob, as the son of Lehi and the author of the book of Jacob, is a figure deeply embedded in the covenantal narrative of the Book of Mormon. His teachings reflect the pure doctrine of Christ, as he emphasizes the importance of faith, repentance, and the coming of the Messiah. The book of Jacob, which contains the record of the Nephilim and the genealogy of Israel, serves as a typological prefiguration of the coming of Christ, illustrating the covenantal relationship between God and His people. Through Jacob's narrative, the Book of Mormon illustrates the fulfillment of ancient prophecies concerning the restoration of the covenant and the establishment of the kingdom of God, thereby connecting Jacob to the eternal covenant and the ultimate revelation of Christ.

name: Nephi
desc: Son of Lehi; visionary prophet; founded the Nephite nation
christ_connection: Nephi, as the son of Lehi and the founder of the Nephite nation, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, embodying the covenantal relationship between God and His people. His visionary prophecies, recorded in [1 Nephi 14:10–13], anticipate the coming of a Messiah who would restore the covenant and bring salvation. Nephi's role in establishing the Nephite community parallels Jesus' role in founding the Church and establishing the gospel, reflecting the continuity of divine purpose through the line of prophets. The covenantal promises made to Nephi, such as the promise of a Redeemer [1 Nephi 13:22], directly connect to the fulfillment of Jesus Christ as the promised Messiah, underscoring the prophetic lineage and the enduring nature of the covenant.

name: Nephi
desc: Son of Helaman; prophet given sealing power; prayed for famine
christ_connection: Nephi, as a prophet given sealing power in the Book of Mormon, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, embodying the role of a seer and messenger who is entrusted with divine revelations. His prayers for famine, as recorded in [1 Nephi 13:23], reflect the broader spiritual struggle and divine intervention that characterize the redemptive work of Christ. Nephi's covenantal relationship with God and his role in conveying divine messages align with the prophetic function of Christ, who is both the fulfillment of ancient promises and the mediator of a new covenant. The spiritual depth and divine authority attributed to Nephi underscore the sacred nature of Christ's ministry and the importance of prophetic leadership in the unfolding of divine purpose.

name: Joseph
desc: Son of Jacob; sold into Egypt; type of Christ
christ_connection: Joseph, son of Jacob, is a figure who typifies the Messiah through his journey of faith and obedience, reflecting the covenantal relationship between God and His people. His experience of being sold into Egypt, where he was reduced to a slave, parallels the crucifixion of Christ, wherein the Son of God was forsaken by His Father. As a type of Christ, Joseph's life demonstrates the suffering and redemption that await the Messiah, fulfilling the prophecy of [Isaiah 53:12] and the covenantal promises made to Israel. His role as a father and provider also underscores the divine provision and care that Christ offers to His people, illustrating the fulfillment of the promise in [Psalm 2:7].

name: Joseph
desc: Youngest son of Lehi; given promises by his father
christ_connection: [Genesis 2:24] Joseph, the youngest son of Lehi, is typified in the covenant of grace, as his birth and early life mirror the promises of Christ, who was also born of a virgin and was promised by his father. [Isaiah 53:1-2] Joseph's lineage is prefigured in the covenant of promise, where God speaks of a descendant who would suffer and rise again, a role that Christ fulfills. [Matthew 1:19] The covenantal promise made to Joseph is fulfilled in Christ, who is the heir of all things and the descendant of the line of David, thereby connecting Joseph's story to the redemptive work of Jesus.

name: Joseph Smith
desc: Prophet of the Restoration; First Vision; received and translated the Book of Mormon
christ_connection: Joseph Smith, as the prophet of the Restoration, points to Jesus Christ through the fulfillment of the covenantal promises made to Israel, particularly in the context of the Book of Mormon. His first vision, which occurred in the wilderness, typifies the divine revelation that Jesus Christ would impart to the Church, as foretold in the Book of Mormon and the Gospels. The Book of Mormon, which Joseph Smith translated, is a prophetic record that connects to Jesus Christ through the covenantal relationship established between God and His people, emphasizing the restoration of the gospel and the reaffirmation of Christ's role as the Savior of the world. The ordinances and doctrines received by Joseph Smith, such as the baptism of the Holy Spirit and the priesthood, are directly connected to the teachings and ordinances of Jesus Christ, underscoring the continuity of the sacred history from the Old Testament to the New.

name: Aaron
desc: Brother of Moses; first high priest of Israel

name: Aaron
desc: Son of Mosiah; missionary to Lamanites; taught the king of the Lamanites

name: Abraham
desc: Father of the faithful; made the Abrahamic covenant
christ_connection: Abraham, as the father of the faithful, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, embodying the covenantal relationship established through the Abrahamic promise [Genesis 12:1-3]. His faith and obedience reflect the moral and spiritual standards that Jesus upholds, fulfilling the role of the "seed of the woman" prophesied in [Genesis 3:15]. The covenantal relationship between God and Abraham, established through the promise of a descendant who would bring salvation [Genesis 12:3], prefigures the redemptive work of Jesus Christ, who is the fulfillment of that promise and the ultimate mediator between God and humanity [Hebrews 4:16]. Abraham's journey from faith to trust in God's word, as seen in his willingness to sacrifice Isaac [Genesis 22:1-14], typifies the sacrificial nature of Christ's atoning death, which is the central act of redemption in the Gospel of John [John 10:11].

name: Saul
desc: First king of Israel
christ_connection: Saul, the first king of Israel, is typified in the covenantal relationship between God and His people, as he initially sought to destroy the worship of the Lord and later became the instrument of God's plan for the redemption of Israel. His transformation from a rebellious king to a prophet of Jesus Christ illustrates the arc of sacred history, where the law given to Moses is fulfilled in the Messiah. The narrative of Saul's journey, marked by divine intervention and moral decay, parallels the spiritual journey of Jesus Christ, who is both the fulfillment of the law and the embodiment of the covenantal promise. [1 Samuel 13:13][Acts 13:26]

name: Solomon
desc: Son of David; built the first temple; renowned for wisdom
christ_connection: Solomon, as the son of David and the architect of the first temple, typifies the ideal of a wise and righteous ruler, reflecting the covenantal promise made to David in [1 Samuel 10:1-21]. His wisdom, as exemplified in [Proverbs 2:6], parallels the divine wisdom of Jesus, who is described as "the wisdom of the Highest" in [Psalm 2:7]. The temple, a symbol of spiritual dwelling and the presence of God, prefigures the heavenly sanctuary that Jesus establishes through his sacrifice in [Hebrews 1:3]. Thus, Solomon's role in the Old Testament serves as a typological precursor to Jesus, who fulfills the covenantal promises and offers eternal salvation.

name: Alma
desc: Priest of Noah who believed Abinadi; founded the church at the waters of Mormon
christ_connection: Alma, as a priest of Noah, was part of the covenantal lineage established by Abraham and extended through the lineage of Israel, thus linking him to the broader narrative of the covenants made with God. His belief in Abinadi and his role in founding the church at the waters of Mormon reflect the establishment of the gospel and the priesthood in the Book of Mormon, which parallels the priesthood of Jesus Christ. The act of founding the church, a foundational ordinance, underscores the importance of the priesthood in the restoration of the gospel and its connection to the eternal covenant with God. This reflects the typological significance of Alma's role in the unfolding of the sacred history leading to the manifestation of Christ.

name: Alma the Younger
desc: Son of Alma; angel-rebuked sinner turned mighty prophet and judge
christ_connection: Alma the Younger, as a figure in the Book of Mormon, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, embodying the virtues of humility, repentance, and divine calling. His narrative in [1 Nephi 17:21–26] illustrates the process of spiritual transformation and the restoration of divine covenantal relationship, mirroring the salvation journey of Christ. The Book of Mormon's portrayal of Alma's struggles and eventual triumph reflects the broader theme of divine grace and the fulfillment of prophecies concerning the coming of the Messiah. Alma's role as a prophet and judge, as depicted in [Alma 13:1–14], underscores the covenantal significance of spiritual leadership and the importance of obedience to divine will, elements that are central to the Christian understanding of Jesus Christ as the ultimate prophet and judge of the world.

name: Ammon
desc: Son of Mosiah; missionary to the Lamanites; defender of the king's flocks
christ_connection: Ammon, as the son of Mosiah and a missionary to the Lamanites, exemplifies the spirit of missionary activity and the defense of religious truth, which are foundational to the gospel of Jesus Christ. His mission to the Lamanites, described in [Book of Mormon: 1 Nephi 1 Nephi 1:14–15], reflects the broader covenantal purpose of spreading the gospel and preserving the commandments, which are central to the doctrine of Jesus Christ. Ammon's role as a defender of the king's flocks, as noted in [Book of Mormon: 1 Nephi 1:16], underscores the importance of maintaining spiritual purity and the covenantal responsibilities inherent in the priesthood and the gospel of Christ. Thus, Ammon's life and actions serve as a typological prefiguration of the missionary work and spiritual defense that Jesus Christ undertakes throughout the world.

name: Peter
desc: Chief Apostle; received keys of the kingdom; also called Simon, Cephas
christ_connection: Peter, the Chief Apostle, is designated as the Rock of Christ [1 Peter 2:4], and his name, Simon, is derived from the Greek word for "rock" [1 Corinthians 10:7]. His role as the "Head of the Church" [1 Corinthians 12:28] and the "Firstfruits of the Spirit" [1 Corinthians 15:53] underscores his prophetic significance, as he is portrayed as the vessel through which the divine promise of salvation is manifested. The symbolism of Peter, often associated with the "Sword of the Spirit" [Ephesians 2:14], reflects his role in the establishment of the Church and the enforcement of the covenantal faith. His experience as a fisherman, transformed into a vessel of salvation, typifies the process of spiritual rebirth and the covenantal relationship between Christ and His people.

name: Joshua
desc: Successor of Moses; led Israel into Canaan
christ_connection: Joshua, as the successor of Moses, exemplifies the covenantal relationship between God and His people, reflecting the enduring nature of the promise made to Abraham. His leadership in leading the Israelites into Canaan parallels the redemptive work of Jesus Christ, who fulfills the covenantal purpose of restoring Israel and bringing salvation to the world. The role of Joshua, as a prophet and leader, typifies the Messiah who would ultimately conquer sin and death, thereby completing the divine purpose of redemption. [Joshua 1:1; Deuteronomy 31:1-3; Psalm 2:7]

name: Captain Moroni
desc: Commander of the Nephite armies; raised the Title of Liberty
christ_connection: Captain Moroni, as Commander of the Nephite armies, is depicted as a figure of authority and leadership, reflecting the broader role of military commanders in the context of covenantal governance. His elevation of the Title of Liberty underscores the covenantal significance of authority and the divine mandate to govern with justice and integrity. This figure typifies the ideal of a righteous leader, aligning with the prophetic vision of a Messiah who shall establish a kingdom of righteousness [Book of Mormon 1:3]. The narrative of Moroni's leadership also connects to the broader arc of sacred history, wherein the establishment of a righteous government is a pivotal step in the fulfillment of divine promises [Book of Mormon 1:4]. The title of Liberty, which Moroni raises, is a covenantal symbol that prefigures the ultimate gift of the Holy Spirit, which is essential for the fullness of the kingdom of God [Book of Mormon 1:5].

name: Moroni
desc: Son of Mormon; sealed the plates; visited Joseph Smith as an angel
christ_connection: Moroni, as the son of Mormon and the seer who sealed the plates, points to Jesus Christ through the fulfillment of the covenant established in the Book of Mormon. His revelation, delivered as an angel to Joseph Smith, typifies the role of Christ as both the mediator and the revealer of divine will. The act of sealing the plates, which is a sacred ordinance, connects to the broader narrative of salvation history, wherein Christ's work is progressively revealed through the prophets and apostles. Moroni's ministry, therefore, serves as a prophetic continuation of the covenantal relationship between God and His people, ultimately pointing to the ultimate revelation of Christ in the Book of Mormon and in the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

name: John the Baptist
desc: Forerunner of Christ; baptized Jesus in the Jordan River
christ_connection: John the Baptist, as the forerunner of Christ, points to Jesus Christ through the covenantal relationship established in the Old Testament, typified in the Mosaic covenant, and fulfilled in the New Testament. His role as the prophet of the Lord, as described in [Matthew 11:1-17], typifies the sacrificial nature of the Messiah, and his baptism of Jesus in [Matthew 3:16] fulfills the prophecy of being the one who would prepare the way for the Lord. The covenantal significance of John's ministry is further emphasized in [Luke 1:35], where the angel announces his role as the messenger of the Lord, connecting him to the divine plan of salvation. His ministry serves as a precursor to the incarnate Christ, illustrating the arc of sacred history from the Law to the Gospel, and his death and resurrection, as foretold in [John 1:29], typify the ultimate sacrifice of the Messiah.

name: King Benjamin
desc: Righteous Nephite king whose address proclaimed Christ's atoning name
christ_connection: King Benjamin, as a righteous Nephite king, serves as a typological figure in the Book of Mormon, emblematic of the coming of Christ. His address, recorded in [2 Nephi 25:1–13], proclaims the atoning nature of Christ's name, mirroring the covenantal promises and the fulfillment of prophecies concerning the Messiah. The Book of Mormon portrays King Benjamin as a precursor to Christ, whose teachings and exhortations anticipate the gospel of Jesus Christ. Through his proclamation of the atoning work of Christ, King Benjamin typifies the role of Christ as the Savior who reconciles humanity to God, fulfilling the covenantal promises made in the Book of Mormon and echoing the prophecies of the Old Testament.

name: Samuel
desc: Prophet, judge, and kingmaker of Israel
christ_connection: Samuel, as the prophet and judge of Israel, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, particularly in the context of the covenantal relationship between God and His people. His role in anointing David to become king parallels the anointing of Jesus as the Messiah, fulfilling the Old Testament promise of a royal descendant of David. The narrative of Samuel's calling and his covenantal responsibilities reflects the broader theological framework of divine sovereignty and the establishment of a new covenant through Christ. The prophetic visions and ethical teachings of Samuel resonate with the moral and spiritual dimensions of Jesus' ministry, illustrating the continuity of divine purpose and the fulfillment of ancient prophecies in the person of Christ.

name: Samuel the Lamanite
desc: Lamanite prophet who prophesied from the walls of Zarahemla
christ_connection: Samuel the Lamanite, as a prophet of the Book of Mormon, serves as a typological figure whose ministry and prophetic functions mirror those of Jesus Christ. His role in foretelling the coming of a Messiah aligns with the biblical concept of a prophet who announces the arrival of a savior, as seen in the ministry of Elijah and the prophecies of Jeremiah. The Book of Mormon records Samuel's vision of the "great and terrible day of the Lord," which parallels the New Testament revelation of the coming of the Messiah, thus establishing a covenantal connection through the fulfillment of ancient prophecies. The spiritual authority and divine commission bestowed upon Samuel reflect the divine appointment of Jesus Christ as the ultimate prophet and mediator of salvation.

name: Paul
desc: Apostle to the Gentiles; formerly Saul of Tarsus
christ_connection: Paul, the Apostle to the Gentiles, is a central figure in the New Testament who points to Jesus Christ through his ministry, teachings, and writings. His mission reflects the covenantal relationship established between God and Israel, as he mediates the promises of the Old Testament to the Gentiles, thereby fulfilling the typological role of the Apostle as a bridge between the Law and the Gospel. Through his letters, Paul emphasizes the sacrificial atonement of Christ and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, which are foundational to the doctrine of salvation. Paul's life and ministry are a continuous revelation of Christ's redemptive work, demonstrating how the covenantal promises of the Old Testament are fulfilled in the person and death of Jesus Christ, and how the New Testament is a continuation of that covenantal narrative.

name: Isaac
desc: Son of Abraham and Sarah; carried the covenant
christ_connection: Isaac, as the son of Abraham and Sarah, serves as a typological figure in the covenantal narrative, embodying the promise of a descendant who would fulfill the covenantal purpose. His birth and role in the covenant mirror the fulfillment of Jesus Christ in the New Covenant, where he is the heir of the promise and the vessel through which God's covenantal intentions are realized. The covenantal relationship established between God and Abraham, typified in Isaac, points forward to the New Covenant in Christ, wherein the same divine promise is enacted through Jesus, who is the ultimate heir and mediator of the covenant. [Genesis 17:1-2; Galatians 3:1-6]

name: Jeremiah
desc: Weeping prophet of Judah; foretold the Babylonian captivity
christ_connection: [Isaiah 53:1-3] Jeremiah, as the weeping prophet of Judah, prefigures the suffering servant of God, whose anguish and sacrifice are typified in the lamentations of the righteous and the covenantal grief of the people of God. [Ezekiel 37:24] The imagery of the valley of Hinnom and the desolation of the city of Jerusalem reflects the prophetic sorrow and the covenantal relationship that would be restored through the redemption of Christ. [Psalm 22:1-14] The psalmist's depiction of the sufferer, who is pierced and laid upon a dunghill, is a direct typology of Jesus, who bore the curse of the law and was crucified in the place of sinners.

name: Adam
desc: First man; father of the human family
christ_connection: Adam, as the first man and father of the human family, points to Jesus Christ through the covenantal relationship established in the beginning. His creation and fall exemplify the moral and spiritual condition of all humanity, foreshadowing the redemptive work of Christ who restores humanity to a right relationship with God. The narrative of Adam's sin and subsequent redemption parallels the salvation of the world through Christ, who is both the descendant of Adam and the fulfillment of the covenantal promise. [Genesis 5:4-5][Genesis 5:24][Genesis 5:3]

name: Noah
desc: Builder of the ark; survived the flood
christ_connection: Noah, as the figure who built the ark and was preserved from the flood, typifies the role of a righteous individual who is entrusted with a divine mission. His act of faith and obedience mirrors the faith of Jesus Christ, who is also entrusted with the mission of salvation. The flood, which destroyed all unfaithful beings, parallels the judgment that will be extended to those who reject God, as seen in the parable of the sower and the destruction of the unfruitful seed. Noah's covenant with God, established through the ark, anticipates the covenant of grace that Jesus Christ fulfills through His atoning work and eternal redemption. The imagery of salvation through faith in a righteous figure, as exemplified by Noah, underscores the theological significance of Jesus Christ as the ultimate mediator and redeemer of the world.

name: King Noah
desc: Wicked Nephite king who burned Abinadi
christ_connection: [Genesis 6:1-2] King Noah, a wicked Nephite king, is depicted as one who burned Abinadi, a prophet of God, and whose actions reflect the consequences of rejecting divine revelation. This figure typifies the broader theme of divine judgment upon those who persist in sin, a principle that is fulfilled in the atonement of Jesus Christ, who offers salvation to all who repent. The covenantal relationship between God and His people, as seen in the story of Noah, is mirrored in the covenant of grace established through Jesus Christ, who is the ultimate mediator between God and humanity.

name: Lehi
desc: Prophet-patriarch who led his family from Jerusalem to the promised land
christ_connection: Lehi, as the prophet-patriarch in the Book of Mormon, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, embodying the covenantal relationship between God and His people. His leadership and faith in the divine promise of the land reflect the covenantal trust and obedience that characterize the spiritual journey of the Church. The narrative of Lehi's journey, marked by trials and divine guidance, parallels the spiritual pilgrimage of Jesus Christ, who is both the fulfillment of the covenant and the ultimate revelation of God's will. The Book of Mormon's portrayal of Lehi thus functions as a prophetic testament, illustrating the continuity between ancient covenantal promises and the redemptive work of Christ.

name: Elijah
desc: Prophet who confronted Baal worship; translated; returned as Elias
christ_connection: Elijah, as a prophet in the Old Testament, points to Jesus Christ through the fulfillment of the covenantal promises and the typological significance of his ministry. His confrontation with Baal worship typifies the spiritual struggle between idolatry and the divine covenant, a struggle that Jesus Christ ultimately addresses through his sacrifice and resurrection. Elijah's role as a messenger of God, his ascension to heaven, and his prophetic function in the prophetic books of the Old Testament all connect to Jesus Christ as the ultimate fulfillment of the promises and the culmination of the redemptive work of the Messiah. [Isaiah 11:10][1 Kings 18:37][2 Kings 2:11]

name: Isaiah
desc: Prophet whose writings are quoted most in the Book of Mormon
christ_connection: Isaiah, as a prophet in the Old Testament, serves as a foundational figure in the covenantal relationship between God and His people, and his writings are frequently cited in the Book of Mormon to illustrate the continuity of divine promises and the fulfillment of ancient prophecies. His typological insights into the coming of the Messiah are evident in passages such as [Isaiah 7:14], where the symbol of a pregnant woman represents the birth of Christ, and in [Isaiah 53:5-6], where the suffering servant typifies Jesus' role in atoning for the sins of humanity. The covenantal language and prophetic structure of Isaiah's writings not only point to the coming of Christ but also serve as a foretaste of the eternal kingdom and the restoration of Israel, reflecting the arc of sacred history leading toward the fullness of God's purpose in Christ.

name: Matthew
desc: Apostle; former publican; author of first Gospel
christ_connection: Matthew, the Apostle and former publican, is designated as the evangelist of the Gospel of Matthew, and his writing serves as a foundational text in the New Testament. His Gospel, [Matthew 1:1], records the birth of Jesus Christ, fulfilling the prophecies of the Old Testament and establishing the covenantal relationship between God and His people. Through Matthew, the narrative of Jesus Christ unfolds as a fulfillment of the promises made to Israel, thereby connecting the typological and covenantal dimensions of Scripture. The emphasis on the "Son of David" and the "Son of Man" in Matthew's Gospel underscores the dual nature of Christ, typifying His role as both the Messiah and the divine Son of God. Thus, Matthew's writings not only point to Jesus Christ as the promised Savior but also serve as a prophetic revelation of the divine plan, anchoring the Christian faith in the continuity of divine revelation.

name: Daniel
desc: Prophet in Babylon; interpreted dreams and visions
christ_connection: Daniel, as a prophet in Babylon, points to Jesus Christ through the covenantal relationship established in the Old Testament, where the Law and the Prophets prepare the way for the Messiah. His visions, such as the image of the ram and the bull, typify the coming of Christ, who is both the Lamb of God and the King of Kings. The book of Daniel, in its prophetic function, connects to Jesus Christ through the fulfillment of eschatological prophecy, where the final judgment and the restoration of Israel are mirrored in the resurrection and eternal kingdom of Christ. The covenantal promises made to Israel, as seen in Daniel’s visions, are fulfilled in the New Covenant through the sacrificial death and resurrection of Jesus, establishing a typological connection that underscores the continuity of divine purpose.

name: Job
desc: Righteous man tested with suffering; affirmed the Resurrection
christ_connection: Job, a figure in the Old Testament, is portrayed as a righteous man tested by suffering, reflecting the human condition of faith amidst trials. His story typifies the covenantal relationship between God and His people, as he is blessed despite his affliction, illustrating the promise of eternal life and the Resurrection. The narrative of Job, with its emphasis on divine justice and mercy, prefigures the redemptive work of Jesus Christ, who, though suffering, is ultimately vindicated and exalted by God, fulfilling the prophecy of the righteous one who suffers and is vindicated. [Job 42:10; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4]

name: Mosiah
desc: Prophet-king; translator of the Jaredite record
christ_connection: Mosiah, as a prophet-king in the Book of Mormon, serves as a typological figure whose role in the covenantal narrative points directly to Jesus Christ. His commission as a translator of the Jaredite record parallels the prophetic function of Christ, who is both the fulfillment of ancient prophecies and the mediator of the new covenant. The emphasis on divine revelation and the restoration of sacred knowledge in Mosiah's ministry mirrors the spiritual mission of Christ, who brings forth the fullness of the gospel and the sealing of the covenant. This figure thus functions as a type of Christ, illustrating the continuity between the Old and New Testament revelations through the lens of covenantal theology.

name: Jared
desc: Brother's unnamed companion; led the Jaredites to the promised land
christ_connection: Jared, as the unnamed companion of Abraham in the Book of Mormon, serves as a typological figure who prefigures the role of Christ in the covenant of grace. His journey, marked by faith and obedience, mirrors the spiritual progression of the Israelites under Moses, who were also guided by divine revelation. The covenantal relationship established between Jared and his people parallels the covenants made between God and His people, emphasizing the continuity of divine promises. The narrative of Jared's leadership and the fulfillment of divine prophecy in the Book of Mormon underscores the enduring nature of the covenant and the redemptive work of Christ through the lineage of the Jaredites.

name: Enoch
desc: Prophet who built Zion; translated without death
christ_connection: Enoch, as a prophet in the Old Testament, serves as a type of Jesus Christ in the sense that he is described as having walked with God and was taken up to heaven without dying, a fact that parallels the resurrection of Jesus Christ. His ascension is a foretelling of the heavenly calling of Jesus, who is also taken up to heaven in a glorified state. Furthermore, Enoch's role in building Zion, a city of God, reflects the heavenly city that Jesus Christ will establish in the new age. The covenantal relationship established between Enoch and God is a prefiguration of the covenantal relationship between Jesus Christ and the elect, where Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant. Enoch's testimony and ascension also point to the importance of faith and the promise of eternal life, which are central tenets of the Christian faith and are exemplified in the life and teachings of Jesus Christ.

name: Gideon
desc: Judge who delivered Israel from Midian
christ_connection: Gideon, the judge of Israel, is typified in Jesus Christ through the imagery of the "heap of broken pieces" and the "stone" that shall be raised [Judg 6:20]. His victory over the Midianites, though achieved through a small army, mirrors Jesus' triumph over sin and death, where the "least" becomes "great" [Mat 10:40]. Gideon's reliance on God's promise, despite human weakness, parallels Jesus' unwavering trust in God's sovereignty, even in the face of despair and doubt [Act 4:24]. The covenantal faith of Gideon, established through divine intervention, anticipates the New Covenant faith in Christ, where the "unworthy" are made "worthy" through the blood of the Lamb [1 Pet 1:10].

name: Helaman
desc: Son of Alma; commander of the stripling warriors; prophet
christ_connection: Helaman, as the son of Alma and commander of the stripling warriors, is typified by the role of a prophet in the Book of Mormon, reflecting the broader covenantal ministry of prophets who proclaim the coming of Christ. His leadership and divine calling mirror the prophetic function of Christ, who is both the ultimate prophet and the fulfillment of all covenantal promises. The covenantal relationship established through Helaman's lineage and service parallels the eternal covenant between God and His people, with Christ as the eternal mediator and redeemer. [2 Nephi 25:22][1 Kings 2:24]

name: Coriantumr
desc: Last surviving Jaredite king; witnessed the destruction of his people
christ_connection: Coriantumr, the last surviving Jaredite king, is typified by Jesus Christ in the sense that both are figures of covenantal significance, entrusted with the responsibility of preserving the lineage of Adam and the covenant of grace. As the last of the Jaredites, Coriantumr's existence and eventual destruction mirror the fate of the Israelites in the Book of Mormon, where the covenant is broken and the people are cast out. This typological connection underscores the theme of covenantal fidelity and the consequences of disobedience, which are also central to the Gospel of John and the Book of Mormon. The narrative of Coriantumr thus serves as a prefiguration of the ultimate covenantal promise made through Jesus Christ, who is both the fulfillment of the covenant and the mediator of the new covenant.

name: Pilate
desc: Roman governor who sentenced Jesus to crucifixion
christ_connection: Pilate, as the Roman governor of Judea, serves as a typological figure within the narrative of Jesus Christ, embodying the archetype of a worldly authority confronted by the Messiah. His role in the crucifixion mirrors the broader theme of divine judgment and the fulfillment of prophecies concerning the Lamb of God. The interaction between Pilate and Jesus reflects the tension between human governance and divine sovereignty, a theme that resonates throughout the New Testament and underscores the crucifixion as a pivotal moment in the redemptive plan of God. [John 19:1-12; 2 Timothy 2:23]

name: Sarah
desc: Wife of Abraham; mother of Isaac
christ_connection: Sarah, as the wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac, serves as a typological figure in the Old Testament, emblematic of the Virgin Mary, the mother of Jesus. Her covenantal relationship with Abraham reflects the foundational covenantal promise extended to all peoples, foreshadowing the redemptive covenant of grace that culminates in Christ. The narrative of Sarah's faith and obedience, as recorded in Genesis 17:15–16 and 21:1–7, parallels the faith and obedience of Mary in her role as the Mother of God, illustrating the continuity of divine purpose and the fulfillment of prophecies concerning the Messiah. The typological significance of Sarah underscores the enduring nature of the covenant and the prophetic anticipation of the incarnate Son of God.

name: Zechariah
desc: Post-exile prophet; messianic visions of the Branch
christ_connection: Zechariah, a post-exilic prophet, is explicitly identified as the messenger of the Lord in [Ezra 4:1], and his visions of the Branch, as described in [Isaiah 11:1-9], typify the coming of the Messiah. His prophecy of the shoot, which is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, reflects the covenantal promise of salvation and the fulfillment of the Davidic lineage. The imagery of the Branch, a central element in Zechariah's visions, is directly linked to the Messiah, who is both the root and the fruit of the covenant, thereby connecting Zechariah's prophetic role to the incarnate Christ through the lens of covenantal typology.

name: Elisha
desc: Successor of Elijah; performed many miracles
christ_connection: Elisha, the successor of Elijah, is typified in the Gospel of John as the prophet who shall be surpassed by Christ, fulfilling the prophecy of [Isaiah 30:3] where it is said, "He shall be a light for the nations, and shall be my servant, to raise up the nations of my people." Elisha's miracles, such as the restoration of the water in Jezreel and the provision of oil for the lamp, are emblematic of the covenantal promises made to Israel, and his death and resurrection (as foretold in [2 Kings 2:10]) points to the ultimate fulfillment of the covenantal purpose in Christ. Thus, Elisha serves as a type of Christ, whose ministry and miracles are prefigured in the Old Testament and whose ultimate destiny is realized in the New Testament through the incarnate Word.

name: James
desc: Apostle; son of Zebedee; brother of John
christ_connection: James, the son of Zebedee and brother of John, is a figure who typifies the role of the apostles in the New Testament, particularly in the context of the covenant of grace. His ministry, marked by faithfulness and leadership, parallels the prophetic role of the apostles as mediators between God and the people. As a companion to Jesus, James exemplifies the covenantal relationship established through the Lord's Supper, where he participated in the ordinance that signifies the body and blood of Christ. Furthermore, James's teachings and writings, such as those in [James 1:1-18], reflect the doctrine of the Holy Spirit and the importance of spiritual growth, which are central to the gospel. The figure of James thus serves as a type of the apostles, whose mission is both a prophecy and a fulfillment of the covenantal promises made to the fathers.

name: Esther
desc: Queen who saved the Jewish people from Haman's plot
christ_connection: Esther, as the queen who saved the Jewish people from Haman's plot, points to Jesus Christ through the lens of divine sovereignty and covenantal faith. Her role exemplifies theantity of the Messiah, as she was chosen by God to intervene in human affairs, mirroring the divine purpose of Christ to redeem and restore. The narrative of Esther parallels the redemptive work of Christ, where God's sovereign action in the midst of human wickedness reflects the ultimate salvation that comes through Jesus, who is both the fulfillment of the covenant and the embodiment of divine grace. [Esther 4:1-7]

name: Laman
desc: Elder son of Lehi; rebellious; progenitor of the Lamanites
christ_connection: [Laman, the elder son of Lehi, is depicted as a figure of rebellion and dissent, reflecting the spiritual and moral failings of the Lamanites, whom Jesus Christ later addresses in the Book of Mormon. His lineage is linked to the covenantal promises made to Lehi and his family, which are foundational to the covenantal relationship between God and His people. Laman's rebellious nature serves as a typological precursor to the spiritual resistance of the world, which Jesus Christ ultimately overcomes through His atoning sacrifice. The covenantal significance of Laman's lineage underscores the enduring nature of the covenant, even in the face of spiritual apostasy, and highlights the divine purpose of Jesus Christ to restore and redeem all who would listen.]

name: Mormon
desc: Nephite prophet-historian who abridged the records
christ_connection: [Mormon] is a Nephite prophet-historian who abridged the records, thereby preserving the covenantal truths of the Book of Mormon. His role as a prophet parallels the function of Jesus Christ in the fulfillment of divine prophecies, as He is both the mediator of the covenant and the revealer of divine will. The Book of Mormon, in its entirety, is a prophetic revelation that points to the coming of Christ, who is the ultimate fulfillment of the covenantal promises made to the Israelites. The abridgment of records by Mormon reflects the spiritual act of interpreting and preserving the covenantal truths, which are ultimately fulfilled in the person of Jesus Christ.

name: Mary
desc: Mother of Jesus Christ; favored of God
variants: Mary the mother of the Lord

name: Simeon
desc: Righteous man who blessed the infant Jesus in the temple

name: Ruth
desc: Moabitess who remained loyal to Naomi; ancestor of David
christ_connection: Ruth, as a figure in the Old Testament, exemplifies the virtue of faithfulness and loyalty in the face of adversity, reflecting the covenantal commitment that underpins the relationship between God and His people. Her story, recounted in [Ruth 1:16], illustrates the theme of divine grace and the enduring nature of the covenant, which is ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ. Ruth's journey from Moab to Israel mirrors the spiritual pilgrimage of the Church, demonstrating how the faithful are called to embrace God's promises despite external trials. This typological connection underscores the role of Ruth as a precursor to the Messiah, whose redemptive work fulfills the promises made to the patriarchs and the covenantal faith of the Israelites.

name: Oliver Cowdery
desc: Scribe to Joseph Smith; received Aaronic and Melchizedek Priesthood
christ_connection: Oliver Cowdery, as a scribe to Joseph Smith and a recipient of the Aaronic and Melchizedek Priesthood, serves as a vital link between the Book of Mormon and the canonical scriptures. His role in the restoration movement reflects the covenantal relationship established between Jesus Christ and the Latter-day Saints, wherein he typifies the faithful servant of God who is called to preserve and proclaim the gospel. The Book of Mormon, in which Cowdery is a key figure, is a prophetic text that points to the coming of Christ and the establishment of the Church, fulfilling the promises of the Old Testament and the New. Cowdery's testimony and writings thus connect to Jesus Christ through the doctrine of the priesthood and the sacred history of the Church, emphasizing the continuity of divine revelation and the importance of obedience to God's commandments.

name: Herod
desc: Ruler who sought to kill the infant Jesus; also Herod Antipas who killed John
christ_connection: Herod, as a figure in the New Testament, serves as a typological representation of the antichrist, reflecting the moral and spiritual decay of the age preceding the coming of Christ. His actions, particularly the massacre of the innocents in Bethlehem, illustrate the consequences of rejecting the divine Messiah and the fulfillment of the prophecy of the Suffering Servant. The figure of Herod is thus a covenantal precursor, whose fate underscores the necessity of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, who alone fulfills the promises of salvation and redemption. [Matthew 2:13-18], [Isaiah 9:1-7], [Revelation 11:7-12].

name: Caleb
desc: Spy who gave a faithful report; inherited Hebron
christ_connection: Caleb, a faithful spy appointed by Joshua to inquire of the land of Canaan, exemplifies the virtue of perseverance in the face of doubt and fear, a quality essential for the disciple of Christ. His report, which affirmed the promise of the land, fulfilled the covenantal assurance of God's faithfulness, thereby typifying the role of the faithful witness who bears witness to the divine truth. As the heir of Hebron, Caleb's lineage is linked to the covenantal inheritance promised to the descendants of Abraham, a lineage that ultimately finds its fulfillment in the eternal seed of Christ, who is the heir of all creation. The narrative of Caleb, recorded in [Joshua 15:5-11], underscores the importance of trust in God's word, a principle that is mirrored in the life and teachings of Jesus, who is the ultimate fulfillment of the covenantal promises.

name: Samson
desc: Judge of Israel; Nazirite of great strength
christ_connection: Samson, as the judge of Israel and the Nazirite of great strength, typifies the Messiah in several ways. His miraculous strength, derived from the Spirit of God, parallels Jesus' divine empowerment through the Holy Spirit. His tragic downfall, marked by his rejection of the divine will and his eventual destruction, reflects the fate of the Messiah who must suffer and be crucified. The covenantal relationship established between God and Samson, symbolized by his Nazirite vow, anticipates the New Covenant through Jesus, who fulfills the promises of salvation and redemption. The narrative of Samson's life, with its themes of divine sovereignty and human frailty, serves as a prophetic framework for the redemptive work of Christ, who is both the fulfillment of the Old Testament promises and the embodiment of the New Covenant's blessings.

name: Ezra
desc: Scribe who led a return from Babylon and restored the law
christ_connection: Ezra, as the scribe who led the return from Babylon and restored the law, typifies the role of a prophet-king in the covenant, for he was both a leader and a custodian of divine revelation. His mission reflects the prophetic function of the Law, which is ultimately fulfilled in Christ, as the Law's purpose is to point toward the Messiah. The restoration of the law, as enacted by Ezra, parallels the re-establishment of the covenant in Christ, where the Law is no longer the ultimate authority but the foundation for the new covenant. Thus, Ezra's actions and teachings connect to Jesus Christ through the lens of covenantal theology, where the Law is both a type and a precursor to the new covenant in Christ.

name: Philip
desc: Apostle from Bethsaida; brought Nathanael to Jesus
christ_connection: Philip, the Apostle from Bethsaida, is depicted as a figure of faith and testimony, whose role in bringing Nathanael to Jesus underscores the theme of divine revelation and the importance of belief in the incarnate Word. His ministry reflects the covenantal relationship between God and His people, as he embodies the prophetic function of proclaiming the coming of Christ. The narrative of Philip's interaction with Nathanael, recorded in [John 1:45-51], illustrates the fulfillment of the prophecy that "a man who was to come is the light of the world" [Matthew 5:14], thereby connecting Philip to the typological significance of Christ as the incarnate light of God. The act of bringing Nathanael to Jesus also highlights the role of the apostles as mediators of divine truth, aligning with the doctrine of the Holy Spirit as the promise of the Spirit [John 15:26], and thus establishing Philip as a vessel through which the covenantal promises are realized.

name: Sam
desc: Son of Lehi; followed Nephi in faithfulness
christ_connection: Sam, the son of Lehi and follower of Nephi, is a figure within the Book of Mormon who typifies the spiritual lineage of Jesus Christ. His faithfulness and obedience to the word of God mirror the virtues and devotion expected of Christ in His ministry. As a descendant of the prophets, Sam's role in the covenant of grace reflects the broader covenantal relationship between God and His people, which is ultimately fulfilled in Christ. The Book of Mormon records Sam's journey of faith, illustrating the progressive revelation of God's plan through the generations, culminating in the redemptive work of Jesus Christ.

name: Micah
desc: Prophet who foretold the birth of Christ in Bethlehem
christ_connection: Micah, the prophet of the Old Testament, is explicitly cited in [Isaiah 7:14] as the one who foretells the birth of Christ, declaring, "Behold, a virgin shall be with child and shall bear a son, and they shall call him Immanuel" ([Isaiah 7:14]). This prophecy is fulfilled in [Matthew 1:18], where the angel Gabriel announces to Mary that she shall bear a son, whom she is to call Jesus, and that he shall be called the Son of the Most High. Thus, Micah's prophecy points to Jesus Christ through the fulfillment of divine promise, establishing a covenantal connection that underscores the fulfillment of ancient foretelling in the New Testament. The reference to Immanuel, meaning "God with us," further ties Micah's prophecy to the incarnation of Christ, affirming the continuity of divine revelation through the arc of sacred history.

name: Abinadi
desc: Prophet martyred by fire; testimony converted Alma; prophesied of Christ
christ_connection: Abinadi, a prophet of the Book of Mormon, is typified by the role of a martyr in the Christian tradition, as he was martyred by fire, a punishment foretold in the Book of Revelation [Revelation 6:9-11]. His testimony, which converted Alma, mirrors the role of the apostles in the New Testament, who were entrusted with the gospel and faced persecution [Matthew 10:19]. Abinadi's prophetic function is also linked to the covenant of grace, as his message was foundational in the development of the Book of Mormon and thus in the broader context of the covenants established through Christ. His martyrdom serves as a precursor to the ultimate sacrifice of Christ, illustrating the fulfillment of prophecy and the continuity of divine revelation.

name: Rebekah
desc: Wife of Isaac; mother of Jacob and Esau
christ_connection: Rebekah, as the wife of Isaac and mother of Jacob and Esau, serves as a typological figure in the Old Testament, emblematic of the motherhood of the Virgin Mary, who is the mother of Jesus Christ. Her covenantal relationship with Isaac mirrors the covenantal relationship between God and Jesus, as both are bound by divine promises and familial ties. The narrative of Rebekah's faith and obedience, as recounted in [Genesis 24:66-73], reflects the spiritual maturity and trust required of Jesus in His role as the Messiah. Furthermore, her role in the birth of the sons who would later inherit the covenant underscores the significance of the lineage through which Jesus is foretold, thus connecting Rebekah to the prophetic fulfillment of Christ's mission.

name: Lemuel
desc: Son of Lehi; followed Laman in rebellion
christ_connection: Lemuel, as the son of Lehi and a figure in the Book of Mormon, serves as a typological representation of the process of spiritual rebirth and the restoration of the covenant. His lineage, marked by rebellion and eventual repentance, mirrors the journey of the faithful who turn from sin to righteousness, reflecting the broader theme of divine redemption. The covenantal relationship established between Lehi and his sons, particularly Lemuel, underscores the importance of faith and obedience in the context of God's plan for salvation. This figure thus points to the necessity of spiritual transformation and the role of divine grace in restoring the covenantal bond, aligning with the prophetic narrative of Christ's redemptive work.

name: Ether
desc: Last Jaredite prophet; wrote the Jaredite record sealed to Moroni
christ_connection: Ether, as the last Jaredite prophet in the book of Mormon, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, embodying the covenantal relationship between God and His people. His writings, sealed to Moroni, reflect the divine purpose of revealing the gospel through successive generations, mirroring the progressive revelation of Christ's ministry and teachings. The book of Mormon's narrative structure, with its emphasis on revelation and the sealing of records, parallels the biblical tradition of divine disclosure, thereby connecting Ether's role to the broader arc of sacred history leading to the manifestation of Christ. [Jacob 4:7; 1 Nephi 13:23; 2 Nephi 25:22]

name: Barnabas
desc: Companion of Paul; son of consolation
christ_connection: Barnabas, as a companion of Paul, exemplifies the covenantal relationship between Jesus Christ and the church, particularly in the context of evangelism and pastoral care. His association with Paul, who was appointed as the apostle to the Gentiles, reflects the typological role of the church as a collective body entrusted with the mission of spreading the Gospel. The narrative of Barnabas in Acts 11:25-26 and 14:1-17 illustrates the prophetic dimension of the church, where individuals are called to bear witness to Christ and to be instruments of His salvation. Furthermore, Barnabas' name, derived from the Greek "bar-nabas," which signifies "son of encouragement," underscores the doctrine of the Holy Spirit's role in empowering believers to proclaim the Gospel, thereby connecting him to the broader narrative of the Holy Spirit's ministry in the New Testament.

name: Timothy
desc: Young companion and protégé of Paul
christ_connection: Timothy, as a young companion and protégé of Paul, serves as a typological figure within the narrative of the New Testament, illustrating the covenantal relationship between God and His people. His calling, as recorded in [2 Timothy 1:1-2], reflects the divine appointment of a servant who is entrusted with the mission of preaching the Gospel, thereby typifying the role of Jesus Christ as the servant of salvation. Timothy's faith and ministry are emblematic of the spiritual inheritance entrusted to the Church, aligning with the prophetic promise of a servant who would preach the word of God [Isaiah 53:12]. Furthermore, Timothy's role in the early church underscores the continuity of the covenantal relationship established through Jesus Christ, wherein the apostles serve as mediators of divine grace, reflecting the sacrificial nature of Christ's redemptive work.

name: Hyrum Smith
desc: Brother of Joseph Smith; martyred at Carthage Jail
christ_connection: Hyrum Smith, as the brother of Joseph Smith, is a figure deeply embedded in the restoration movement, which is rooted in the Book of Mormon. His martyrdom at Carthage Jail exemplifies the covenantal commitment required of those who uphold the gospel, as emphasized in [Book of Mormon: 1 Corinthians 10:1-11], where the act of faith and sacrifice is portrayed as essential to the covenantal relationship. Hyrum's death serves as a typological precedent, reflecting the ultimate sacrifice of Jesus Christ, as depicted in [Hebrews 10:12-14], where the sacrificial offering is presented as the fulfillment of the law. Furthermore, his role in the restoration underscores the prophetic significance of the Book of Mormon, which is seen as a revelation of the same divine plan that was revealed through Jesus Christ, as proclaimed in [Matthew 24:14].

name: Thomas
desc: Apostle; doubted then testified of the risen Christ
christ_connection: Thomas, the Apostle, is a figure who exemplifies the transformation of faith from doubt to certainty, mirroring the divine process of salvation. His initial doubt, expressed in [John 20:11], reflects the human condition of uncertainty in the presence of the risen Christ, yet his subsequent testimony, recorded in [John 20:24-29], demonstrates the fulfillment of the promise of resurrection and the power of the Holy Spirit in convicting the heart. As a disciple, Thomas's journey typifies the broader narrative of the New Testament, where faith is cultivated through trials and revelation, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of Christ's redemptive work. His role in the Gospel of John underscores the importance of personal experience and the covenantal relationship established between God and His people, affirming the divine nature of Jesus Christ and the efficacy of the sacraments of the Church.

name: Amos
desc: Prophet who cried for justice and righteousness
christ_connection: [Isaiah 5:20] Amos, as a prophet of the Old Testament, is typified in the New Testament by Jesus Christ, who is the fulfillment of the covenant promises made to Israel. The call of Amos to proclaim justice and righteousness, as recorded in [Amos 5:4], mirrors the ministry of Jesus, who is the embodiment of the covenant of grace. The prophecy of Amos concerning the destruction of the wicked and the salvation of the righteous, as seen in [Amos 2:12], parallels the parable of the sheep and the goats in [Matthew 25], where Jesus distinguishes between the just and the unjust. Thus, Amos serves as a type of Christ, whose mission and message are ultimately centered on the restoration of justice and the salvation of the people of God.

name: Jonah
desc: Prophet sent to Nineveh; sign of Christ's burial and resurrection

name: Eve
desc: First woman; mother of all living
christ_connection: Eve, as the first woman, is depicted in Genesis 3:20 as the mother of all living, and her fall in Genesis 3:18 is emblematic of the broken covenant established with Adam in Genesis 2:16-17. Her disobedience serves as a typological precursor to the sin of the Son, illustrating the consequences of transgression and the necessity of redemption through Christ. The covenantal relationship between God and Eve, as outlined in Genesis 3:15, foreshadows the sacrificial atonement required for the restoration of fellowship with God, a theme central to the New Testament narrative. The figure of Eve, thus, functions as a type through which the eternal covenant and the redemptive work of Christ are mediated, reflecting the arc of sacred history from original sin to salvation.

name: Lazarus
desc: Raised from the dead by Jesus; brother of Mary and Martha
christ_connection: Lazarus, the figure who is raised from the dead by Jesus, points to the fulfillment of the divine promise made in the Book of John, Chapter 11, Verse 35, where it is declared that "God has shown his power through the resurrection of the dead." This event typifies the broader covenant of salvation, wherein the death and resurrection of the Messiah serves as the inauguration of the new covenant. The narrative of Lazarus's resurrection connects to the doctrine of the Lord's Supper, as it illustrates the sacrificial nature of Christ's death and the promise of eternal life through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, Lazarus's story is part of the prophetic sequence leading to the Messiah, demonstrating the arc of sacred history in which the Son of God is both the fulfillment and the beginning of the new covenant.

name: Titus
desc: Companion of Paul; leader of the church in Crete
christ_connection: Titus, as a companion of Paul and leader of the church in Crete, exemplifies the pastoral care and doctrinal integrity essential to the Christian faith. His role in the early church reflects the covenantal commitment to preach the gospel and build up the body of Christ, as emphasized in [Ephesians 4:11-16]. Titus' leadership underscores the importance of spiritual maturity and moral conduct, which are foundational to the Christian life and the fulfillment of the promises made through Christ. His example serves as a typological precursor to the church age, illustrating the continuity of God's plan for salvation and the necessity of faithful leadership in the service of Christ.

name: Miriam
desc: Sister of Moses; prophetess of Israel
christ_connection: Miriam, the sister of Moses and prophetess of Israel, is typified in Jesus Christ through the imagery of the "burning bush" and the "plagues" she witnessed, which are emblematic of the divine presence and redemptive work of Christ. Her role as a prophetess parallels Christ's prophetic ministry, where He proclaimed the word of God and led the people toward salvation. The covenantal relationship established between God and Israel, as exemplified by Miriam's leadership and divine commission, is fulfilled in the New Covenant through Christ's redemptive sacrifice and eternal priesthood. The narrative of Miriam's death in the wilderness, a tragic yet redemptive event, mirrors the crucifixion of Christ, where the faithful are ultimately delivered from bondage through the sacrifice of their Redeemer.

name: Nehemiah
desc: Governor who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem after the exile
christ_connection: Nehemiah, as a figure of covenant and restoration, points to Jesus Christ through the lens of divine redemption and the fulfillment of the Old Testament promises. His role in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem mirrors Jesus' mission to restore the broken relationship between God and humanity, typifying the sacrificial act of redemption that underlies the covenant. As a leader who overcame obstacles to bring about divine purpose, Nehemiah's story echoes Jesus' perseverance in the face of adversity, illustrating the continuity between the Old and New Testament narratives. The covenantal significance of Nehemiah's work parallels the New Covenant established through Jesus, where both serve as agents of God's will in the salvation of the people.

name: Andrew
desc: Apostle; brother of Peter; first called
christ_connection: Andrew, the brother of Peter, is a figure of profound significance in the New Testament, serving as the first of the Twelve Apostles and the first to be called by Jesus. His role as a companion to Peter and his eventual martyrdom exemplifies the sacrificial nature of the faith, reflecting the covenantal relationship between Jesus and His disciples. The narrative of Andrew's call, recorded in [John 1:40-42], underscores the divine initiative in the selection of disciples, aligning with the broader theme of Jesus' mission to gather a spiritual community. His life and death typify the ultimate sacrifice required for the salvation of humanity, thus connecting him to the prophetic fulfillment of Christ's redemptive work.

name: Martha
desc: Sister of Mary and Lazarus; received testimony of the Resurrection
christ_connection: Martha, the sister of Mary and Lazarus, is depicted in the Gospel of Luke as one who believed in the resurrection, and her testimony is recorded in [Luke 16:31]. Her faith is typified by the biblical concept of the "faith of the world" and is connected to the broader narrative of the resurrection, which is a central tenet of Christian theology. Her example is a testament to the importance of faith in the face of death and is thus linked to the covenantal promise of salvation through Jesus Christ, as the resurrection is both a fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy and a foundational doctrine of the New Testament. Martha's testimony is a prophetic echo of the ultimate resurrection, which is the culmination of the redemptive work of Christ, and her role underscores the significance of the covenantal relationship between God and humanity, particularly in the context of the New Covenant.

name: Brother of Jared
desc: Powerful prophet; saw the finger of God; shown all things
christ_connection: Brother of Jared, as a prophet in the book of Mormon, serves as a type and prefiguration of Jesus Christ, whose ministry and revelations are mirrored in his prophetic visions. His experience of seeing the "finger of God" and being shown all things aligns with the divine revelations that Jesus Christ imparted, fulfilling the covenantal promises made through the lineage of prophets. The book of Mormon's portrayal of Brother of Jared underscores the continuity between ancient prophetic traditions and the New Testament revelations, establishing a spiritual lineage that points toward the ultimate fulfillment of divine will in Christ.

name: Hannah
desc: Mother of Samuel; her prayer is a model of faith
christ_connection: Hannah's prayer, recorded in [1 Samuel 1:11], exemplifies the depth of faith and trust in God's sovereignty, reflecting the covenantal relationship established between God and Israel. Her lamentation, "[1 Samuel 1:11] For I am despised; yet I will not be forsaken," illustrates the typological significance of the mother of Jesus, as she embodies the ideal of a woman who relies wholly on God's promise, even in times of despair. This figure connects to Jesus through the covenantal promise of salvation, as Hannah's faith anticipates the coming of the Messiah, who would bring salvation to all nations [Isaiah 49:15]. Her prayer thus serves as a prophetic model, illustrating the enduring nature of God's covenant and the hope it brings, even in the darkest of times.

name: Nathanael
desc: Apostle in whom there was no guile; also called Bartholomew
christ_connection: Nathanael, the Apostle and son of Philip, is a figure who points to Jesus Christ through the lens of covenant and typology. His initial doubt and subsequent faith reflect the spiritual journey of the disciple, illustrating the transformative power of divine revelation. As the beloved disciple of Jesus, Nathanael's narrative in John 1:45-51 serves as a typological prefiguration of the ultimate disciple who would believe in Jesus despite initial skepticism, thereby embodying the covenantal promise of faith and the fulfillment of prophecy. This connection is further reinforced by the New Testament's emphasis on Nathanael as a model of spiritual discernment and the fulfillment of the covenantal covenantal promises.

name: Deborah
desc: Judge and prophetess of Israel
christ_connection: Deborah, the judge and prophetess of Israel, is typified in Jesus Christ through the lens of divine sovereignty and deliverance. Her role as a leader in the covenantal community mirrors Christ's role as the Messiah, who fulfills the promises of salvation and restoration. As a figure of faith and courage, Deborah's life parallels the spiritual journey of believers, emphasizing the importance of faithfulness and divine guidance. Her prophetic utterances, such as the song of Deborah [Judg. 4:28], resonate with the prophetic voice of Christ, who is both the fulfillment of ancient promises and the source of spiritual revelation. The covenantal relationship established through Deborah's leadership reflects the eternal covenant between God and His people, which is ultimately centered in Christ.

name: Ezekiel
desc: Prophet among the exiles in Babylon; vision of the valley of dry bones
christ_connection: Ezekiel, as a prophet among the exiles in Babylon, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, particularly in the context of the covenantal imagery and the restoration of Israel. His vision of the valley of dry bones, [Ezekiel 37:1-14], typifies the spiritual condition of the people of God, who, like the dry bones, were spiritually lifeless and in need of divine resurrection. This imagery parallels the resurrection of Jesus, who, as the incarnate Son of God, brings life to the dead and restores the covenant relationship between God and His people. The covenantal promise made to Ezekiel, [Ezekiel 37:24], which speaks of the renewal of the people and the outpouring of the Spirit, directly connects to the New Covenant established through Jesus Christ, who is the fulfillment of the promises made to Israel. Thus, Ezekiel's prophetic role is both a type and a prophecy of the Messiah, who brings about the full realization of the covenantal hopes.

name: Malachi
desc: Last Old Testament prophet; prophesied Elijah's return
christ_connection: Malachi, the last Old Testament prophet, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, particularly in the context of the covenantal relationship between God and Israel. His prophecies, such as those concerning the "abomination of desolation" [Malachi 1:14], foreshadow the sacrificial nature of Christ's atonement, aligning with the sacrificial offerings of the Old Testament. Furthermore, Malachi's emphasis on the importance of maintaining a holy and faithful relationship with God parallels the spiritual discipline and moral integrity required of believers in the New Testament. The covenantal promises made to Israel through Malachi, such as the assurance of divine blessing and the call to repentance, find their fulfillment in the redemptive work of Jesus Christ, who embodies the culmination of the covenantal promise and the restoration of relationship with God.

name: Zoram
desc: Servant of Laban who joined Lehi's family and was a free man

name: Hosea
desc: Prophet whose marriage symbolized God's covenant with Israel

name: Stephen
desc: First Christian martyr; saw Christ at the right hand of God
christ_connection: Stephen, the first Christian martyr, is a figure who points to Jesus Christ through the lens of covenant and prophecy. His witnessing of Christ at the right hand of God [Acts 4:10] fulfills the Old Testament promise of a Messiah who would be crucified and raised again [1 Peter 2:21]. Stephen's death exemplifies the sacrificial nature of Christ's redemptive work, as he is stoned and slain for his faith, mirroring the ultimate sacrifice of Jesus. His martyrdom also typifies the culmination of the sacrificial covenant between God and Israel, wherein Christ becomes the new Aaron, offering Himself as the eternal high priest [Hebrews 5:1-5]. Thus, Stephen's life and death are intricately connected to the redemptive plan of God, illustrating both the typological and prophetic dimensions of Christ's mission.

name: Caiaphas
desc: High priest who condemned Jesus
christ_connection: Caiaphas, as the high priest who condemned Jesus, serves as a typological figure within the Old Testament framework, reflecting the broader covenantal relationship between God and Israel. His role as a high priest, a position of spiritual authority, parallels the ministry of Jesus, who is both the Messiah and the High Priest of the New Covenant. The condemnation of Jesus by Caiaphas echoes the prophetic warnings against the rejection of the Messiah, as foretold in [Isaiah 53:3], and underscores the tension between the Old and New Covenants. Caiaphas' actions thus typify the ultimate judgment and the fulfillment of the prophecy of the suffering servant, pointing to the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

name: Nicodemus
desc: Pharisee who came to Jesus by night; learned of being born again
christ_connection: Nicodemus, a Pharisee who came to Jesus by night, is a figure who exemplifies the concept of being "born again" as described in [John 3:1-21]. His journey reflects the covenantal promise of spiritual rebirth, which is a central tenet of Christian theology. The act of coming by night symbolizes the hidden nature of the divine grace that occurs beyond the visible and the conventional, aligning with the idea of the Holy Spirit's work in the heart of the believer. This figure typifies the role of a disciple who, though initially outside the fold, is drawn into the covenant of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, thus connecting to the broader narrative of salvation and the fulfillment of the Old Testament promises through the New Testament figure of Christ.

name: Emma Smith
desc: Wife of Joseph Smith; first president of Relief Society
christ_connection: Emma Smith, as the wife of Joseph Smith and the first president of the Relief Society, serves as a typological figure within the broader narrative of the Restoration. Her role exemplifies the covenantal relationship between God and His people, as she embodies the ideal of a devoted wife and mother, reflecting the divine promise of spiritual nourishment and guidance. Her life and leadership are intertwined with the prophetic vision of the latter days, where she is depicted as a vessel through which the gospel of Jesus Christ is disseminated and cherished. The scriptural context of her ministry is grounded in the covenantal promises of the Book of Mormon and the Book of Revelation, wherein she is portrayed as a servant of the Lord, fulfilling the role of a prophetess and a leader in the restoration of the gospel.

name: Sariah
desc: Wife of Lehi; mother of Nephi; murmured then believed
christ_connection: Sariah, the wife of Lehi and mother of Nephi, serves as a typological figure within the Book of Mormon, emblematic of the faithful woman who trusts in divine revelation. Her narrative parallels the spiritual journey of Christ, wherein she initially murmurs doubts but later embraces faith, reflecting the transformative power of divine truth. As a mother, she embodies the covenantal role of nurturing faith in future generations, a theme that resonates with the Church's mission to disciple and teach. The Book of Mormon's portrayal of Sariah underscores the importance of personal conviction and the covenantal promises made to those who remain steadfast in their faith, mirroring the eternal covenants of Christ.

name: Zacchaeus
desc: Chief publican who climbed a tree to see Jesus
christ_connection: Zacchaeus, the chief publican, is typified by the archetype of a repentant sinner, reflecting the broader moral and spiritual transformation that Jesus embodies. His act of climbing a tree to see Jesus illustrates the divine accessibility of Christ, aligning with the covenantal promise of salvation through faith. This figure connects to Jesus through the lens of the New Covenant, wherein the servant of the Lord is portrayed as one who repents and surrenders to God, thereby fulfilling the prophecy of the "Lamb of God" who takes away the sin of the world [John 1:29]. Zacchaeus' story also underscores the theme of redemption through grace, a central tenet of the Gospel of Luke, where the inclusion of a Gentile in the Kingdom of God is celebrated [Luke 19:1-10].

name: Brigham Young
desc: Second prophet; led pioneer exodus to Utah; colonized the West
christ_connection: Brigham Young, as the second prophet of the Restoration, serves as a typological figure within the broader narrative of divine revelation and covenantal fidelity. His leadership during the exodus to Utah reflects the covenantal promises made to Abraham, wherein the seed of the promise was to be brought forth in a land of promise. The exodus, akin to the Israelite journey, underscores the divine purpose of bringing the chosen people into a new covenant, mirroring the redemptive plan of God as revealed in the Old Testament. Furthermore, Young's role in establishing the Church in the West parallels the prophetic ministry of Jesus Christ, who, as the Lamb of God, was sent to redeem the world, a role that Young embodied through his mission and teachings. The covenantal relationship between Young and the Lord, as seen in the Book of Mormon, typifies the eternal covenant between God and His people, a covenant that Jesus Christ fulfills in His redemptive work.

name: Sherem
desc: Anti-Christ who confronted Jacob and was struck by God
christ_connection: Sherem, as a figure in the Book of Mormon, serves as a typological precursor to Jesus Christ, embodying the antichrist who opposes the true gospel of Jesus Christ. His confrontation with Jacob reflects the broader struggle between the false prophet and the true prophet, mirroring the conflict between the antichrist and the Christ in the last days. Sherem's fate—being struck by God—symbolizes the ultimate judgment upon those who reject the true Messiah, aligning with the prophecy of the final judgment and the restoration of true faith. This figure thus typifies the antichrist who will arise in the last days, fulfilling the covenantal promise of the Lord's work in the latter days.

name: Joseph of Nazareth
desc: Husband of Mary; earthly guardian of Jesus
christ_connection: Joseph of Nazareth, as the earthly guardian of Jesus, typifies the role of a righteous and faithful guardian in the covenant of grace, reflecting the divine promise of salvation through faith. His life, marked by obedience and humility, parallels the sacrificial nature of Christ's redemptive work, illustrating the fulfillment of the Old Testament covenantal promises. As the progenitor of the Messiah, Joseph's narrative connects to the prophetic expectation of a servant who would bear the sins of the world, thus establishing his role as a type of Christ in the sacred history of salvation.

name: Anna
desc: Prophetess who recognized the infant Jesus in the temple
christ_connection: Anna, a prophetess who recognized the infant Jesus in the temple, points to Jesus Christ through the lens of divine revelation and covenantal fidelity. Her recognition reflects the fulfillment of the prophecy in [Isaiah 7:14], where the virgin birth is foretold, and her identification with the infant Christ underscores the typological significance of the Mosaic covenant. Anna's role exemplifies the prophetic function of women in the biblical narrative, as seen in the broader context of the Spirit's work in the church, and her experience aligns with the divine promise of the Messiah's incarnation. The narrative of Anna's encounter with Christ thus connects to the overarching theme of the covenantal relationship between God and His people, emphasizing the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies in the New Testament.

name: John
desc: Beloved Apostle; translated; author of Revelation and the Gospel of John
christ_connection: John, as the beloved Apostle and author of the Gospel of John and Revelation, serves as a vital conduit through which the divine nature of Jesus Christ is revealed. His writing typifies the covenantal relationship between God and humanity, emphasizing the incarnate Son as the Lamb of God who suffers for the sins of the world [John 1:29]. The prophetic content of John's Gospel, particularly in the Book of Revelation, anticipates the ultimate redemption of the faithful and the establishment of the Kingdom of God [Revelation 21:1-7], thereby connecting to the fulfillment of Christ's redemptive work. John's role as a prophet and interpreter of divine truth underscores the continuity between the Old and New Testaments, illustrating the arc of sacred history in which Jesus Christ is both the incarnate Word and the final revelation of God's eternal plan.

name: Mary Magdalene
desc: First witness of the resurrected Christ
christ_connection: Mary Magdalene, as the first witness of the resurrected Christ, points to Jesus Christ through her role as the first to encounter Him after His resurrection. Her testimony is foundational, as she is the sole witness who directly addresses Christ in the resurrected state, thereby fulfilling the prophecy of the "woman who bore John" (John 20:14). Her narrative is intertwined with the covenant of grace, as she is portrayed as the "one who was promised" (Luke 1:38), and her experience typifies the fulfillment of the promise of salvation. Her story connects to Jesus Christ through the ordinance of baptism, as she is the first to be baptized by John the Baptist (Luke 3:21), and her role is emblematic of the New Covenant, where she is the first to proclaim the risen Lord.

name: John the Revelator
desc: Translated Apostle; key figure in the Restoration of the priesthood
christ_connection: John the Revelator, as the Translated Apostle and key figure in the Restoration of the priesthood, points to Jesus Christ through the restoration of the Aaronic priesthood and the reestablishment of the covenantal relationship between God and His people. His role is typified in the Book of Mormon, where he is depicted as a prophet who receives revelations from God to guide the restoration of sacred ordinances and the fulfillment of ancient prophecies. The Book of Mormon chapter 1:1–3 and the Book of Revelation chapters 1:1–20 serve as the textual foundation for this connection, illustrating how John's ministry mirrors the prophetic role of Jesus Christ in the latter days, emphasizing the continuity of divine revelation and the restoration of spiritual truth.
